messages.subject: lmer with residualised predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

We're having issues understanding what happens when one factor is residualised against another.
The scenario is this: as predictors we have expert rating data for pronunciation features and corresponding rating data from potential employers, as part of a study of what might influence judgments of acceptability-for-employment of migrant workers.
Since the two sets of ratings are correlated, we have residualised employer ratings against the corresponding expert ratings, and included expert ratings and residualised employer ratings in an lmer model predicting acceptability scores. We have also run a parallel model with non-residualised employer ratings. Let's call these models Resid and Nonresid respectively.
Our understanding was that residualisation tells us what aspects of, in this case, employer ratings are unique over and above expert ratings. We were therefore surprised that the coefficients, p-values etc for the employer ratings are identical in the two models (i.e. regardless of whether it is the residualised or non-residualised employer ratings that are used). Pleasingly, the effects of the expert ratings are significant in model Resid (as they are also when modelling without employer ratings at all), whereas they were not in model Nonresid (which we assume is due to the competition between the correlated employer and expert ratings).
So our question is this - should we have expected the effects of employer ratings to be different depending on whether they are residualised or not? And if we should, what might explain the fact that they are identical in our two models?

Thanks

Paul

Paul Warren
  Associate Professor in Linguistics, School of Linguistics and Applied Language Studies (VZ320)
  Associate Dean (PGR), Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences (MY312)
Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand

messages.subject: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.subject_clean: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I posted this on stackoverflow last week but got no answer, maybe someone
on this list would know? If so, it would be wonderful!

I am running the following model. I am defining "repetition" as an ordered
factor as it has the values 1, 2, 3, and 4. context and lat are categorical
non-ordered factors. lmer automatically calculates whether or not
repetition has a quadratic, cubic, and ^4 effect on my dependent variable.
I am however not interested in these terms and am worried these may take
away some of the variance for nothing. Does anyone know how I could avoid
having these extra terms calculated? Any help would be much appreciated!!

messages.subject: Re: lmer with residualised predictors
messages.body_plain:
Exactly. As Wurm & Fisicaro discuss (and Matt points out), residualizing
one predictor by another or including both predictors in a model
achieves the same (in what concerns the residualized predictor).

>         Pleasingly, the effects of the expert ratings are significant
>         in model Resid (as they are also when modelling without
>         employer ratings at all), whereas they were not in model
>         Nonresid (which we assume is due to the competition between
>         the correlated employer and expert ratings).

This is also to be expected. At least in the two-predictor case:
1. Y ~ X1
2. Y ~ X1 + X2
3. Y ~ X1.resid + X2
4. Y ~ X1 + X2.resid

If I read W&F right, the estimate for X1 should be the same in models 2
and 3, but also the estimate for X1 should be the same in models 1 and
4, because common variance between X1 and X2 is now totally attributed
to X1.

Best,
João

On Thu, Oct 16, 2014 at 11:59 PM, Stephanie Ries
<stephanie.ries.cornou-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
> Hi all,

> I am running the following model. I am defining "repetition" as an ordered
> factor as it has the values 1, 2, 3, and 4. context and lat are categorical
> non-ordered factors. lmer automatically calculates whether or not repetition
> has a quadratic, cubic, and ^4 effect on my dependent variable. I am however
> not interested in these terms and am worried these may take away some of the
> variance for nothing. Does anyone know how I could avoid having these extra
> terms calculated? Any help would be much appreciated!!

This happens because ordered factors are still treated as factors --
and a factor with 4 levels creates 3 or 4 degrees of freedom
(depending on whether there's an intercept).

To avoid this, tell R to treat the predictor as a number:
  y ~ context * as.numeric(repetition) + lat + (1 | name)

-n

-- 
Nathaniel J. Smith
Postdoctoral researcher - Informatics - University of Edinburgh
http://vorpus.org

messages.subject: Re: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.subject_clean: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.body_plain:
Alternatively, because polynomial contrasts are the default for ordered
factors, you could change the contrasts of the factor (for example, to
treatment contrasts):
contrasts(repetition) <- contr.treatment(4)

Or "repetition" could still be treated as a factor, but unordered (in
which case treatment contrasts would be applied by default):
repetition <- factor(repetition, ordered=F)

When making "repetition" numeric, and given that it enters into an
interaction with context, I would center it.

Hope this helps,
João

messages.subject_clean: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Oct 17, 2014 at 12:30 AM, João Veríssimo <jl.verissimo-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
> Alternatively, because polynomial contrasts are the default for ordered
> factors, you could change the contrasts of the factor (for example, to
> treatment contrasts):
> contrasts(repetition) <- contr.treatment(4)
>
> Or "repetition" could still be treated as a factor, but unordered (in
> which case treatment contrasts would be applied by default):
> repetition <- factor(repetition, ordered=F)

This will still result in 3 different betas for the 'repetition' term,
though, and possibly less interpretable ones. (In particular, there
won't be any linear term at all.)

That said, I'd be inclined to leave the full set of polynomial
contrasts in. They're constructed to be orthogonal to the linear
contrast, so it's unlikely that they're going to take any variance
from it -- and even if they do, that's probably a good thing. There's
some discussion of this in

Smith, N. J. and Kutas, M. (in press), Regression-based estimation of
ERP waveforms: I. The rERP framework. Psychophysiology. doi:
10.1111/psyp.12317

> When making "repetition" numeric, and given that it enters into an
> interaction with context, I would center it.

Yeah, generally a good idea! If you use a polynomial contrast for a
factor then the ".L" term is centered automatically, but if you're
using a numeric predictor then you have to center by hand.

-- 
Nathaniel J. Smith
Postdoctoral researcher - Informatics - University of Edinburgh

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie,

First of all, make sure that your variable repetition is numeric (e.g., as.numeric(as.character(repetition)) if it is a factor). Then you can use poly(repetition, 1) to only receive the linear polynomials. As in lmer(y ~ context * poly(repetition, 1) + lat + (1 | name), dt). The number indicates the degree of the polynomial.

However, I would also compare it with a fit to the numjeric variable.

Hope this helps,
Henrik

messages.subject: Re: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.subject_clean: How to drop non-linear terms for ordered factors in lmer?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephanie,

After some discussion with Daniel Ezra Johnson offlist I realized that the only thing poly(..., 1) does is center the variable (and scale it to some scaling constant). Basically it only changes the interpretation of intercept (which is then evaluated at the mean of repetition) and the scaling of the slope.

But given that you have repetition in an interaction it makes sense to center it. As otherwise the main effects would be so-called simple effects (e.g., http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/65898/442). However, this centering could also be achieved using scale(repetition, scale = FALSE) which would have the benefit of not changing the interpretation of the slope (as it would still be on the original scale).

I would also strongly advise to center the other variables and if they are categorical use contr.sum for them. Otherwise the main effects could be difficult to interpret.

The other take home message for me is to only use poly() if one want to use more than linear polynomials. Then the function comes in handy.

Cheers,
Henrik
